extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and legal researchers interested in Canadian constitutional and criminal law
extracted.subtask_description: Wikipedia article summarizing the Supreme Court of Canada decision R v Zundel (1992) about the constitutionality of the Criminal Code prohibition on spreading false news and its interaction with section 2(b) (freedom of expression) and section 1 (justification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 181 (spreading false news) — statutory offence elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "[e]very one who wilfully publishes a statement, tale or news that he knows is false and causes or is likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment" (Section 181, Criminal Code, as quoted on page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording sets the legal elements the Crown must establish for conviction: wilful publication, knowledge of falsity, and causation or likelihood of causing injury/mischief to a public interest. The provision was the subject-matter of the constitutional challenge in R v Zundel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irwin Toy test for section 2(b) protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court applied "the test established in Irwin Toy Ltd v Quebec (AG)" and found section 181 met both elements of that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated on the page: first element — the Court observed that "all form of speech is protected unless it is violent" (so content is generally protected); second element — there was "government action aimed at curbing such expression" (i.e., the law targeted expression). The test is used to decide whether expression falls within s.2(b) protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1 justification — requirement of an ascertainable purpose/objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court found "there was no evidence to the purpose or objective underlying section 181" and rejected the Crown's attempt to rely on a "shifting purpose" toward promoting "social harmony."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision emphasizes that, for a limit on expression to be justified under s.1, an objective must be demonstrable and supported by evidence; courts "cannot assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived current utility of the impugned provision." Lack of an identifiable purpose weighs against s.1 justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality / minimal impairment / overbreadth concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority held the restriction on all expressions "likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest" was "far too broad," and therefore could not be justified under section 1 of the Charter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treated the statutory breadth of the prohibition as failing the proportionality/minimal impairment aspects of s.1 analysis: a law that captures a wide range of non-harmful expression cannot be justified merely by asserting a general benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissenting approach: content neutrality, social harmony objective, rational connection and minimal impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissenting judges noted section 2(b) "safeguards all forms of non-violent expression" (content neutral) and used section 15 and section 27 of the Charter to support the objective of section 181 as promoting "social harmony." The dissent found a "rational connection" and minimal impairment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the dissent's framework, the objective (social harmony) is legitimate and the law is not overly impairing because the Crown must prove specific elements (willful publication and likely to cause injury). This shows an alternative s.1 balancing outcome based on different factual/legal weightings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary indicators of falsehood in published material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court "thoroughly examined the book in question and determined that it 'misrepresented the work of historians, misquoted witnesses, fabricated evidence, and cited non-existent authorities'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual findings are examples of the kinds of documentary indicators courts may rely on to conclude a publication is false or fraudulent when assessing offences or assessing the content at issue in constitutional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof burden for conviction under section 181 (as described by dissent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissent noted that conviction required the Crown to prove the accused "willfully published false materials, and the statement was likely to cause injury to the public interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reiterates the mens rea and causation/likelihood components of the statutory offence and explains why the dissent considered impairment of expression to be limited by the required evidentiary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness grounds for ordering a new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Appeal ordered a new trial because of "errors in the conduct of the trial, particularly regarding jury selection and misdirection on elements of the offence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies procedural-legal criteria (improper jury selection, misdirection on legal elements) that can invalidate a trial verdict and justify retrial — relevant to evaluations of trial fairness and grounds for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing consideration — evidence of community impact
rubrics_metrics.description: District Court Judge Thomas noted the sentence was less severe because he could not find evidence that Zündel was able to have a "significant part of the community react to his beliefs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentencing may take into account empirical evidence of the publication's actual community impact; lack of demonstrable effect can reduce perceived harm and mitigate sentence severity.
